questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Medical jurisprudence: negligence, consumer protection, PC-PNDT, MTP & transplantation acts
questions.stem: The four essential elements to establish medical negligence are:
options: Duty of care, breach of duty, causation and damage
questions.concept: All four elements must be proved; a poor outcome alone is not negligence. The standard applied is that of a reasonably competent practitioner of the same standing - the Bolam test.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Medical jurisprudence: negligence, consumer protection, PC-PNDT, MTP & transplantation acts
questions.stem: Res ipsa loquitur, meaning the thing speaks for itself, applies when:
options: The injury could not have occurred without negligence, such as a swab left in the abdomen
questions.concept: The burden of proof shifts to the doctor in such cases - a retained instrument, wrong-site surgery or a burn from a diathermy pad, where negligence is self-evident and expert evidence is unnecessary.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Medical jurisprudence: negligence, consumer protection, PC-PNDT, MTP & transplantation acts
questions.stem: Under the Consumer Protection Act, medical services are covered except when:
options: The service is rendered entirely free of charge to all patients
Treatment is in a government hospital
questions.concept: Following Indian Medical Association v V P Shantha, paid medical services fall within the Act. Services free to everyone are excluded, but if some patients pay, even those treated free are covered.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Medical jurisprudence: negligence, consumer protection, PC-PNDT, MTP & transplantation acts
questions.stem: Vicarious liability means:
options: An employer is responsible for the negligent acts of employees in the course of employment
questions.concept: Under respondeat superior, a hospital is liable for negligence by its staff. Contributory negligence, where the patient's own conduct contributes to harm, may reduce the damages awarded.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Medical jurisprudence: negligence, consumer protection, PC-PNDT, MTP & transplantation acts
questions.stem: Under the amended MTP Act, termination of pregnancy up to 20 weeks requires the opinion of:
questions.concept: One practitioner suffices up to 20 weeks and two from 20 to 24 weeks for specified categories including survivors of rape and minors. Beyond 24 weeks, a state medical board decides in cases of substantial fetal abnormality.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Medical jurisprudence: negligence, consumer protection, PC-PNDT, MTP & transplantation acts
questions.stem: Under the PC-PNDT Act, the offence committed by disclosing the sex of the fetus is punishable for:
options: Both the person conducting the test and the person seeking it
questions.concept: The Act penalises the practitioner, the clinic and those seeking sex determination, with imprisonment and fine and suspension of registration. Clinics must register, maintain Form F records and display prohibition notices.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Medical jurisprudence: negligence, consumer protection, PC-PNDT, MTP & transplantation acts
questions.stem: Under the Transplantation of Human Organs Act, brain-stem death must be certified by a board of:
options: Four doctors including the registered medical practitioner in charge and a neurologist or neurosurgeon
questions.concept: The board must not include the transplant team, avoiding conflict of interest. Two sets of tests are performed six hours apart, and the Act permits organ retrieval after brain-stem death certification with authorisation.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Medical jurisprudence: negligence, consumer protection, PC-PNDT, MTP & transplantation acts
questions.stem: Professional secrecy may be breached without patient consent when:
options: There is a statutory duty or an overriding public interest, such as notifiable disease or court order
questions.concept: Privileged communication permits disclosure to the appropriate authority when public interest outweighs confidentiality - notifiable diseases, court directions, or a driver or pilot with a dangerous condition after counselling refusal.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Medical jurisprudence: negligence, consumer protection, PC-PNDT, MTP & transplantation acts
questions.stem: Consent for a surgical procedure in India must be:
options: Informed and written, obtained from a person 18 years or older
questions.concept: For examination, implied or oral consent may suffice; for any procedure involving risk, informed written consent is required covering nature, risks, benefits and alternatives. Loco parentis applies for minors in emergencies.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Medical jurisprudence: negligence, consumer protection, PC-PNDT, MTP & transplantation acts
questions.stem: A doctor may examine an accused person at the request of the police under:
options: Section 53 of the Criminal Procedure Code, using reasonable force if directed
questions.concept: CrPC Section 53 permits examination of an arrested person at police request, and Section 53A specifically for rape accused. Consent is not required, distinguishing it from consensual clinical examination.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: Under Indian law, the essential element constituting rape is:
questions.concept: The law requires penetration without valid consent; rupture of the hymen, injuries or semen are corroborative but not essential. Absence of injury never excludes rape and this must be clearly stated in the report.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: The age of consent for sexual intercourse in India is:
options: Eighteen years, below which consent is legally irrelevant
questions.concept: Sexual activity with anyone under 18 constitutes an offence under the POCSO Act regardless of apparent consent, and reporting of such cases by a doctor is mandatory under Section 19 of that Act.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: The two-finger test in examining a rape survivor is:
options: Prohibited, being unscientific and a violation of dignity
questions.concept: The Supreme Court and Ministry of Health guidelines have banned the per-vaginum two-finger test and any comment on habituation to sexual intercourse, as it is scientifically meaningless and re-traumatising.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: Infanticide is defined as:
options: The unlawful killing of a child under one year of age
Killing of a fetus in utero
questions.concept: Feticide is destruction of the fetus in utero, infanticide is killing of an infant under one year, and the key medico-legal question is whether the child was born alive and had a separate existence.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: The hydrostatic (flotation) test at autopsy is used to determine:
options: Whether the infant breathed after birth, by testing whether the lungs float
questions.concept: Aerated lungs float, indicating live birth. False results occur with putrefaction, artificial respiration or freezing, so it must be interpreted alongside lung histology and other signs of separate existence.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: Signs indicating that a newborn had a separate existence include:
options: Aerated lungs, air in the stomach and changes in the umbilical cord
questions.concept: Establishing live birth requires evidence of respiration and of independent survival - lung expansion with the diaphragm at the fifth or sixth rib, air in the gastrointestinal tract, and cord and ductus changes.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: Sodomy under Indian law after the 2018 Supreme Court judgment:
options: Is no longer an offence between consenting adults in private
Remains an offence in all circumstances
Is an offence only for men
questions.concept: Navtej Singh Johar v Union of India read down Section 377 to decriminalise consensual acts between adults; non-consensual acts, acts with minors and bestiality remain offences.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: In examining a suspected rape survivor, the most important medico-legal principle is:
options: Obtaining informed consent, maintaining chain of custody of samples and documenting objectively
questions.concept: The doctor documents findings and collects evidence; whether rape occurred is a judicial determination. Treatment, emergency contraception, STI and HIV prophylaxis and psychological support must not be delayed for legal formalities.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: Criminal abortion is distinguished from a lawful MTP by:
options: Being performed outside the conditions and by persons not authorised under the MTP Act
questions.concept: Lawful termination requires an approved indication, an authorised registered medical practitioner and an approved place. Outside these, it constitutes an offence under the Indian Penal Code even if performed by a doctor.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: The commonest cause of death in criminal abortion is:
questions.concept: Unsafe abortion by untrained persons causes fatal haemorrhage, sepsis, uterine perforation and, less commonly, air embolism or vagal inhibition. It remains a leading contributor to maternal mortality in India.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: The medico-legal significance of vital reaction in a burn is that it:
options: Indicates the burn was sustained during life rather than after death
Determines the cause of the fire
questions.concept: Antemortem burns show a red line of hyperaemia, vesicles with high protein and chloride content and inflammatory infiltration, whereas postmortem burns lack these vital reactions - crucial in distinguishing burning to conceal homicide.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: In a death from a house fire, the finding that proves the victim was alive during the fire is:
options: Soot in the trachea and bronchi with raised carboxyhaemoglobin
questions.concept: Inhaled soot below the vocal cords and blood carboxyhaemoglobin above about 10% prove respiration during the fire. Their absence suggests death occurred before the fire started.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: Pugilistic (boxer) attitude in a burnt body is caused by:
options: Heat coagulation of muscle proteins causing flexor contraction, occurring in both antemortem and postmortem burning
questions.concept: Because heat stiffening occurs regardless of whether the person was alive, this posture has no value in determining whether burning was antemortem, a common examination point.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: Under Indian law, a dying declaration recorded from a burns victim:
options: Is admissible even without a magistrate, provided the person is conscious and oriented
questions.concept: A dying declaration is admissible under Section 32 of the Indian Evidence Act; certification of fitness of mind by the doctor is important, and recording by a magistrate carries greater evidentiary weight but is not essential.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: Joule burns (electric marks) at the site of electrical contact are characteristically:
options: Firm, pale, depressed lesions with raised margins and no vital reaction of inflammation
questions.concept: The endogenous heat generated at the contact point produces a nodular pale crater with peripheral areola. Metallisation of the skin from the conductor may be demonstrated chemically and helps identify the object.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: The commonest cause of immediate death in low-voltage electrocution is:
questions.concept: Domestic alternating current at 50 Hz readily induces ventricular fibrillation. High-voltage current more often causes respiratory centre paralysis and extensive deep burns with the victim thrown clear.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: Filigree (arborescent) burns are pathognomonic of:
questions.concept: Lisichenko or fern-like marks are transient superficial ferning patterns from electron showers along the skin. They fade within hours, so early photography is essential, and are diagnostic of lightning.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A scald differs from a flame burn in that a scald:
options: Spares the hair and shows no charring or singeing, with splash marks and dripping pattern
questions.concept: Moist heat below 100 degrees cannot singe hair or char skin, so preserved hair with a trickling pattern indicates a scald, important in distinguishing accidental from inflicted injury in children.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: In suspected dowry death, the medico-legal importance of examining the pattern of burns lies in:
options: Distinguishing accidental kitchen burns from homicidal kerosene burns by distribution and smell
questions.concept: Kerosene-soaked homicidal burns typically involve the trunk and back with an inverted distribution, whereas accidental cooking burns spare the back. Section 304B applies to unnatural death of a woman within seven years of marriage.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: Heat stroke is characterised by:
options: Core temperature above 40 degrees with altered mental state and absent sweating
questions.concept: Failure of thermoregulation with hot dry skin, confusion and multi-organ dysfunction distinguishes heat stroke from heat exhaustion, which has intact sweating. Immediate aggressive cooling is life-saving.
